# Workspace releases

The root `pi-roundtable` package and every `packages/*` workspace share one version.
Drawing, coding, web, sandbox, and MCP live here with their full original Git history; webchat started here.
A single `v<version>` tag runs `publish.yml`: the existing core job checks the entire tree and publishes the core, then a matrix publishes each workspace independently.
The matrix is generated by `scripts/check-release.ts` and includes all six workspaces.
The root's `files` allowlist does not include `packages/`.

## Development

Run `bun install --frozen-lockfile` at the repository root.
After changing workspace manifests, remove root and workspace `node_modules` before installing: Bun 1.4.2's incremental relinking can leave child-local core links pointing at the child itself.
The workspace linkage regression test fails on such stale links.
If they persist after a clean install, rebuild `bun.lock` from scratch with Bun 1.4.2 and review the newly resolved dependencies: its older lockfile format can retain invalid nested root entries.
The committed lockfile uses the current format; clean installation and repeated frozen installation both pass the linkage regression.
Bun does not treat the root package as a child workspace; the root-only `pi-roundtable: link:.` override and hoisted linker give every workspace a live symlink to the core.
Workspace manifests use ordinary semver for both the core development dependency and its peer range.
No workspace or local-path dependency specifier is shipped in a workspace manifest.
A consuming project ignores the root package's development override.

Run core checks with `bun run typecheck`, `bun run lint`, and `bun run test`.
Run all workspace checks with `bun run check:packages`.
Run `bun run --cwd packages/web build` to build the console assets.
CI performs these checks with PostgreSQL and native canvas prerequisites installed, including MCP's PostgreSQL tests.
Sandbox's Docker integration is opt-in locally; CI explicitly enables it on the native Linux Ubuntu runner with its local Docker daemon and non-root runner account:

```sh
(cd packages/sandbox && SANDBOX_DOCKER_TEST=1 bun test src/docker.integration.test.ts)
```

CI and the core publication gate both run this test and require the native Linux, non-root, opt-in conditions rather than accepting a skipped test.
The test keeps the production isolation flags and credential broker intact.
Docker Desktop on macOS is not an execution substitute because it does not share host Unix sockets into Linux containers.

## First publication and trust

These are owner actions, not part of the migration.
Use Node 24 and npm 11.15 or newer, enable account 2FA, and log in with browser/security-key authentication using `npm login`.
Core `0.7.0` and its original `v0.7.0` tag already exist; this migration leaves that release commit unchanged.
Drawing, coding, and web `0.7.0` are already published and trust this repository's `publish.yml`.
The core's existing trust stays on `publish.yml`.
No package-specific tags or workflows are used.

### Sandbox's first publication

Check the migration commit's CI before publishing sandbox.
From the repository root, install and run the checks above, then publish the new package manually:

```sh
(cd packages/sandbox && npm publish --access public --provenance=false)
```

Local publication disables provenance because provenance is generated by supported CI environments, not a developer's shell.
The package must exist on npm before trusted publishing can be configured:

```sh
npm trust github pi-roundtable-sandbox --file publish.yml --repo wayne930242/pi-roundtable --allow-publish
```

### Webchat's first publication

pi-roundtable-webchat is new in 0.8 and does not exist on npm yet (`npm view pi-roundtable-webchat` answers E404), so the `v0.8.0` tag's preflight stops before the core publishes until the owner publishes it once by hand.
The tag must still publish webchat `0.8.0` itself, with provenance, so the hand publication uses a prerelease version that the tag never publishes.
Do it from the `0.8.0` release commit after its CI passes, before pushing the tag:

```sh
cd packages/webchat
# Temporarily, and never committed: a prerelease placeholder that only creates the package.
npm pkg set version=0.8.0-0
npm publish --access public --provenance=false --tag first-publish
git checkout package.json
npm trust github pi-roundtable-webchat --file publish.yml --repo wayne930242/pi-roundtable --allow-publish
npm trust list pi-roundtable-webchat
```

Then run `bun scripts/preflight-release.ts v0.8.0` without `--local`: it now finds the package.
Push the tag; `publish.yml` publishes webchat `0.8.0` through OIDC as `latest`.
Afterwards remove the placeholder's tag and mark it unusable:

```sh
npm dist-tag rm pi-roundtable-webchat first-publish
npm deprecate pi-roundtable-webchat@0.8.0-0 "placeholder for the first publication; use 0.8.0 or later"
```

Do not publish webchat `0.8.0` by hand: the tag's webchat job would then fail on the existing version, and the release would have no provenance.

### MCP's trust migration

MCP already exists on npm at `0.4.1`, so it needs no manual publication.
Its version jumps to lockstep `0.7.0`, with peer range `>=0.7.0 <0.8.0`, tested against core `0.7.0`; the public API and package name stay unchanged.
The owner moves its trust from the old repository after the migration commit's CI passes and before the next lockstep tag.
These commands follow `npm help trust` in npm 11 (which is not workspace-aware):

```sh
npm trust list pi-roundtable-mcp
npm trust revoke pi-roundtable-mcp --id=<old-trust-id>
npm trust github pi-roundtable-mcp --file publish.yml --repo wayne930242/pi-roundtable --allow-publish
npm trust list pi-roundtable-mcp
```

Replace `<old-trust-id>` with the ID listed for the old repository.
The registry supports only one trusted publisher per package, so revoke the old configuration before creating the new one.
Do not revoke it until the migration and shared workflow are ready.
Verify the final list names this repository and `publish.yml`, then add a moved notice to the old repository and archive it.
Do not manually publish MCP `0.7.0` or recreate the existing `v0.7.0` tag: the next new lockstep tag publishes the version recorded by that tag, including MCP.
A subsequent patch tag such as `v0.7.1` publishes MCP `0.7.1` with core 0.7.x compatibility; a minor tag such as `v0.8.0` publishes MCP `0.8.0` instead.
The current `0.7.0` migration manifest does not require an intervening registry release.
Until that next tag publishes, npm's MCP `0.4.1` does not support core 0.7.x; the migrated API is available in this checkout only.
`scripts/preflight-release.ts` checks package existence by name, not whether the new version is already published, so the existing MCP `0.4.1` satisfies its first-publication gate.

## Subsequent lockstep releases

Update the root version and every workspace version together.
Update every workspace's core development dependency to that version and its peer range to the matching minor, for example `>=0.8.0 <0.9.0` for `0.8.0`.
Update changelogs, regenerate `bun.lock`, and run the clean-install checks and packing checks.
Run `bun scripts/check-release.ts v0.8.0` before committing: it refuses mismatched versions, core peer ranges, development pins, and repository directories.
Run `bun scripts/preflight-release.ts v0.8.0`: it packs every workspace, checks required files (including the web HTML/JS/CSS, drawing fonts, and sandbox worker sources), and requires each package to exist on npm before the core can publish.
Use `--local` only for CI or pre-first-publish checks, where a new package need not yet exist on npm.
For `v0.8.0`, pi-roundtable-webchat needs [its first publication](#webchats-first-publication) first.
Verify every workspace's trusted publisher is configured against this repository's `publish.yml` before pushing a release tag; package existence alone does not prove OIDC authorization.
Commit and push, wait for CI for that exact commit, then have the owner push the single `v0.8.0` tag.
`publish.yml` checks all versions before any publication and publishes all packages with provenance through npm OIDC.
If a package job fails after other packages publish, rerun only the failed jobs rather than republishing the successful core or packages.
Do not use Re-run all jobs: npm refuses to overwrite the already-published core version, stopping the downstream matrix.
Publication across multiple npm packages is not atomic; pack/existence preflight cannot guarantee registry availability or OIDC authorization.
